## PM ruling: **(A)** — `$search` emits `$icontains` for textual fields. Dispatching. ⚠️ Veto window, not a permission gate.

Claim: PM loop round 5
Session: `session_01VGAePF7iGGUYUT8oX1cVgx`
Branch: `claude/issue-7641-search-case-insensitive`
Worktree: `objectstack-issue-7641`
Domain: `domain:engine-core`
File surface: `packages/objectql/src/search-filter.ts` (+ the three declarations, + shared conformance coverage)
Container & model: M, `mode:cloud`, `model: opus`
Serial constraints cleared: `search-filter.ts` untouched by everything that landed this shift — #7868 (`8b90d68`) changed `search-companion.ts` + `engine.ts` only, **not** this file, so it did not cover this card. `search-companion.ts` free since #7868 merged. No engine-core card in flight

### Why this is the PM's call and not yours

The card flags the A/B direction as the maintainer's. Applying the escalation bar, I'm ruling it instead, and I want the reasoning on the record so it can be vetoed cheaply:

**Three separate places already declare case-insensitive** — the `cross-field-object-search` checklist item title, `search-filter.ts`'s own docblock (*"Matching: case-insensitive"*), and the `search-conformance` ledger row. That makes this **declared ≠ enforced**, which the loop names as a restore-invariant class: the repo has already stated the invariant, so the finding that it is broken carries its own decision. Option B is not a symmetric alternative — it is rewriting three declarations to match a behaviour nobody chose, produced incidentally when #6518's SQLite `LIKE`→`GLOB` change removed an accidental ASCII fold.

⛔ **This does not touch #4706 Q2.** `$contains` stays contractually case-sensitive. The change is *which operator `$search` compiles to*, not what either operator means — so the ruling is orthogonal to however #4706 finally lands. That is what makes it safe for me to decide.

**Veto window**: if you'd rather have (B), say so and I'll stop the dispatch — but I'm not waiting on it.

### Compile-surface check, run before dispatch rather than assumed

Because this changes which operator a filter compiles to, the per-surface question is *"does this surface implement `$icontains` at all?"* — a surface that doesn't would make search silently break or refuse there. Re-verified at HEAD (⛔ not copied from the reference table):

| # | surface | `icontains` hits |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | `driver-sql` (+ sqlite-wasm / turso-local by inheritance) | 23 |
| 2 | turso `RemoteTransport` (independent compiler) | 19 |
| 3 | service-analytics `read-scope-sql` | 2 |
| 4 | service-analytics `filter-normalizer` | 1 |
| 5 | `formula` `matches-filter` | 7 |
| ½ | objectql `having-filter` | 15 |

Control check passed (`$contains` present in the same files), so the counts are real. **All six support it** — the blocking risk is absent. ⚠️ But 4 and 3 are thin enough (1 and 2 hits) that a count could be a mention rather than an implementation; the dev declares each surface explicitly rather than inheriting my grep.

`driver-memory` / `driver-mongodb` are **frozen** (#5499): declare, conclude "out of scope + #5499", ⛔ do not flip.

## ACCEPTED on the merits — ⏸️ flip HELD until `TypeScript Type Check` reports its own conclusion.

At `9fc2f9d`: **ESLint success** (03:47:20Z); **TypeScript Type Check is still `in_progress`** (started 03:42:55Z). Everything else green, 25 of 26 concluded. ⛔ I am not flipping on "nothing has failed yet" — reading an aggregate instead of the job's own `conclusion` is precisely how #7833 got flipped ready while two gates were red earlier this shift. Flip fires the moment TypeScript concludes `success`.

All three of your open questions: **approved as you judged them.** Reasoning below so the record shows they were decided, not waved through.

### 1. The select raw-value fallback — you read past the literal wording, correctly

The ruling said "textual fields" and the card said enum/select is "already unaffected". Both were true *of the `$in` path*, which you left alone. The **raw-value fallback** is a different arm: an operator clause compared against raw stored text. Leaving it on `$contains` would have kept the docblock's unqualified *"Matching: case-insensitive"* **partly false** — which is the exact defect class this card exists to close.

You also stayed inside the ⛔ that mattered: it is the search compiler's **output**, not an operator's implementation. **Keep it.** Flagging it as the one judgment call rather than burying it is what made it cheap for me to affirm.

### 2. searchAll — in scope, and splitting it would have been worse

Not scope creep: `search.console-global-search`'s `knownGaps` **already recorded that the palette path shares this defect and that #7641 owns it**. The card's real boundary was written down somewhere other than the card, and you found it.

Splitting it out would have left a **fourth false declaration** live — a comment asserting *"ObjectQL exposes case-insensitive substring matching via `$contains`"* — for however long the follow-up card took. Fixing a contract in one producer while a second producer keeps contradicting it is not a smaller change, it is an incoherent one. **Keep it.**

### 3. No palette e2e — right call, and the honesty is the point

You pinned `searchAll` at the emitted-filter level and said plainly that an end-to-end palette assertion would need the search plugin's route booted, which no dogfood test sets up. ⛔ Claiming HTTP-level coverage you don't have would have been the failure here. The per-object `$search` path **does** have it, and you drew that line explicitly. Noted; no action.

### What makes this report unusually good

**The compile-surface sweep answered my caveat instead of inheriting it.** I handed you grep counts and warned that faces 3 and 4 (1–2 hits) might be mentions rather than arms. You verified by *reading each implementation*: face 3's thin count was a compact arm folding **both** sides; face 4's single hit was a **map entry**, which you then chased downstream to confirm both renderers honour the cube op. A count cannot distinguish a mention from an arm — you said so and acted on it.

Declaring `having-filter` explicitly **because** `FILTER_LOGIC_CASES` doesn't drive that path is the same instinct: the face where a miss goes green is the one that most needs stating.

**The reverse-verification is the best I've seen this shift.** Reverting each producer *independently* — 7 red / 1 red / 3 red — and the detail that on the dogfood revert the **4 pre-existing cases stayed green** doesn't just prove your test works; it *reproduces the blind spot the card described*, in the same run.

**And the root cause of that blind spot:** several downstream fake matchers *folded both sides while keyed on `$contains`* — implementing `$icontains` semantics under the case-sensitive operator's name. That is why no unit test on this path ever caught it, and annotating each one means the next author meets the explanation.

Two more things I'd have accepted a worse answer on: keeping `__search` on `$contains` (lowercase column × lowercased term ⇒ a case-sensitive operator is *exact*, not a bug) **and pinning that the two clauses deliberately use different operators so nobody "aligns" them later**; and declining to add rows to `FILTER_TEXT_CASES` because that table is about operator *semantics*, which did not move.

Also noted: you found the shared checkout sitting on this branch and detached it to `origin/main` before working in a dedicated worktree. That was my local checkout — correct handling, and no `git stash`.
